title: Sell Mineral Rights in Sullivan County, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Sullivan County, PA
metaDescription: Sullivan County minerals leased but never drilled? We buy Marcellus interests here, explain what held-by-production actually means, and pay cash.
heroLead: Sullivan County is the quiet neighbor in the Marcellus story. It got leased just as hard as Bradford and Susquehanna counties next door, but a lot of that ground has sat undeveloped for years, and that quiet is exactly what confuses owners the most.
intro: Sullivan County is one of the least populated counties in Pennsylvania, tucked into the Endless Mountains with the county seat in Laporte, a borough small enough that most people drive through it without noticing. During the Marcellus leasing rush of the late 2000s, landmen covered this county thoroughly, and thousands of acres got locked into five-year primary terms with the same operators drilling hard in Bradford and Susquehanna counties. But Sullivan County's terrain is steeper, its access roads thinner, and its population base smaller, so a meaningful share of those leases expired or sat quiet while operators concentrated rigs on easier ground nearby.

That history leaves a lot of Sullivan County families in an unusual spot. Some own minerals under an active, producing unit that pays like any other Marcellus interest. Others hold a lease that technically expired years ago and never got formally released, or a fresh lease that's still sitting in its primary term with no well anywhere near it. Knowing which situation you're actually in changes everything about what your interest is worth.

sections.heading: Leased Doesn't Always Mean Drilled Here
paragraphs: In a county like Sullivan, the gap between a signed lease and an actual producing well can run years, sometimes indefinitely. If your family signed a Marcellus lease during the boom and no well was ever drilled on your unit before the primary term expired, that lease may no longer be valid at all, which means your minerals could be entirely open to a new lease today. On the other hand, if a well was drilled and completed on your unit before the primary term ran out, most standard leases stay held by production for as long as that well keeps producing, even at modest rates.

We check this first on every Sullivan County inquiry, because it changes the entire conversation. An unleased, open interest in a lightly developed county is worth something different than a producing interest tied to an active unit, and neither number is something you should guess at.

sections.heading: The Deduction and Impact Fee Questions Still Apply
paragraphs: For the Sullivan County families who do have an active, producing interest, the same statewide rules govern the check. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets the one-eighth floor on gross value, and post-production deductions for gathering and compression can still be applied within that calculation depending on how your specific lease was written, the same Kilmer v. Elexco framework that governs leases across the play. Act 13 impact fees also reach Sullivan County, funding township roads and emergency services, but that money flows from operator to local government, not into your royalty statement.

sections.heading: Terrain, Access, and Why Development Has Been Slower Here
paragraphs: Sullivan County's steep ridges and state game lands make well pad construction and pipeline routing more expensive than in flatter counties nearby, and that cost difference has kept the pace of drilling here noticeably slower than in Bradford or Susquehanna County even though the rock itself sits in the same dry-gas fairway. Operators have tended to prioritize acreage where infrastructure already exists, which means Sullivan County activity often clusters near the county line where it connects into gathering systems built for the neighboring county's wells.

sections.heading: What We Look at Before Making an Offer Here
paragraphs: Because status varies so much parcel to parcel in Sullivan County, we spend extra time confirming whether your lease is still in force, whether a well has actually been drilled on your unit, and what the DEP's permit records show for anything nearby. From there we give you a clear, honest number, whether that's for a producing interest, an expired-lease open interest, or something in between. We record every transfer properly with the recorder of deeds in Laporte.

faqs.question: My family leased minerals in Sullivan County years ago but nothing was ever drilled. Is the lease still active?
faqs.answer: Possibly not. Most leases from that era had a five-year primary term, and if no well was drilled and completed before that term expired, the lease likely lapsed. We can help you check the recorder of deeds records to confirm.

faqs.question: If my lease expired, can I still sell my minerals?
faqs.answer: Yes. An expired lease often means your minerals are unleased and open, which is a different value situation than a producing interest, but it still has value and we buy interests in that condition.

faqs.question: Why is there so much less drilling in Sullivan County than Bradford or Susquehanna?
faqs.answer: Steeper terrain, more limited road and pipeline access, and a smaller population base made development costlier here, so operators have generally prioritized acreage with existing infrastructure in neighboring counties first.

faqs.question: Does state game land nearby affect my private mineral interest?
faqs.answer: Not directly. State game lands are managed separately by the Pennsylvania Game Commission, and if your minerals are under private land, ordinary lease and ownership rules apply regardless of what's next door.

faqs.question: Do impact fees apply if there's no active well on my specific unit?
faqs.answer: Act 13 impact fees are assessed per unconventional well, so if there's no well on your particular unit, there's no fee tied to it. Fees collected elsewhere in the county still fund township infrastructure broadly.
